[b]My playtime:[/b] I played this offline, but i think it took somewhere around 12-24h to finish the game.
[b]Grindy Achievement:[/b] No.
[b]Optional Achievement:[/b] Yes (8 achievements).
[b]Difficult Achievement:[/b] No.
[b]Developer Response:[/b] No (last response is in 26 Feb, 2019).

[h1]Intro[/h1]
Hacknet is a hacking simulator game where you have to hack some ip address with the tools you had. Most of the hacking will be done through terminal although the game has some GUI that you can interact with.

[h1]Graphics[/h1]
Even though i said that you'll type your commands through terminal, it doesn't mean that you'll only have to look at it. There are some UI in the game that you can see, such as when you launch your tools or check the compromised system. I even think that the UI helped very well because i'm sure i don't want to browse all of the system directory from the command line; it took too much effort to type and check them all. You can also see the server location and connect to them without typing at all in case you forgot the ip or just too lazy to type the whole thing.

[h1]Story[/h1]
The game's story is mostly told through an exchange of emails and reading files in a server. You'll investigate someone who has been lost for a long time, Bit, while uncovering a hidden secret that causes his disappearance. The story might look decent, but i'm quite impressed with the visuals at the end of the story.

The game also has additional files in the servers that you hacked in. I like to read some of them (especially the short ones) since they are pretty funny.

[h1]The game[/h1]
As a hacking simulator game, the game simulates the terminal very well. The basic is pretty much the same (ls, cd, cat, etc) while there are some custom commands mixed in. The game also has an auto complete feature although it's quite limited; you can't do auto complete for stuffs in other directory. Well, sometimes it works, but sometimes it don't. The game also doesn't support complicated command with arguments like rm -rf (remove everything in a directory) even though the game has missions like this. The limitations are pretty acceptable to me though.

Anyway, if you have no idea with anything that i said above, the game will help you to learn some terminal commands. If you're in windows, it's the thing that popped up when you press windows+r and then type cmd, except that the commands are for Linux OS and the like. Like how most terminals are, there is a help command that you can use to recognize all of the available commands and if you didn't notice it like i did, the help command actually has paging in it; you can type help 1, help 2, and help 3 to check most of the commands in the game. Most, because the help command won't tell you anything about what does your .exe file do.

Beside the basic commands, you'll also have .exe files. These files are usually what is installed in your computer and can be basically anything, from a browser to your game. However, most .exe files in this game is actually a tool that is used for hacking. You'll know how the things work if you read the instructions, which is obviously stored somewhere else. You'll usually get these .exe files by going through some servers and copying the files to your machine.

In this game, you'll need to read a lot. By a lot, i mean a lot. Really. You might need to understand some complicated stuffs or just know the general knowledge and the game will punish you severely if you don't know what are you doing. I mistook proxy servers and port for a while and i thought that i need 4 proxy servers to hack in a server although it actually asked me to open 4 ports. I got confused for a while before i noticed my mistake.

Sometimes, the game won't tell you what to do and you had to understand everything by yourself. One example is when a hacker suddenly attacked me. I didn't know what to do at that point because the tutorial (yes, there is a tutorial) only tells me how to hack.

As i said before, you'll usually hack a server. You'll have a lead in a form of ip address that you need to hack in and you'll check what you need to do to hack it. The game will usually tell you whether you have to connect to a proxy, guess a firewall, run one of your hacking tools to open a number of port required to get in, or all of them. Sometimes, the server owner will notice your break in and a timer will show up. You must finish your hacking, remove your traces, and logout before it reaches zero or you'll get a blue screen. The strange thing is, the game is a bit "buggy" on this. If you leave the server while running your hacking tools, the hacking will still be ongoing and you can do your second attempt with a head start. The stranger thing is, if the timer reach zero by the time you finish the hacking (and you haven't logged out yet), the hacking will also be finished after you deal with the blue screen and return to the server. Well, there are actually some more, but these two are the only thing that i had in my mind for now.

Since you'll use a lot of hacking tools, you might run out of memories. Some hacking tools take more memories than the others so you can't use them all at the same time. This helps to make the game more difficult although there is one place where you have to "cheat" your way through because you will never have the time to get in in the first place [spoiler](the CCC Hacksquad Filedump)[/spoiler].

The game's story has a two branching paths that will converge in the end. The other path requires you to really know what you're doing though; i won't be able to make it in if i didn't read a guide beforehand. The game also has some commands that are not available in help commands that might be useful in these cases. These additional commands are told after you beat the game and is supposed to be an additional command in case there is a new update in.

You'll mostly play the game by accepting quests and finishing them. There is also a few points in the game where you can choose the missions that you want to do. Sadly, there is a place where you can't choose them all and it kinda saddens me since it left the place with unfinished tasks.

Since you'll be hacking a lot of servers, there are some optional places that you can go to and some places might have some secrets in it. I had fun locating a lot of new servers that are not introduced in the main story although i'm not sure if i got all of them; sometimes, the secret is so well hidden that you have to read really carefully.

Pros:
- Uses mostly real terminal commands
- 2 branching paths
- Lots of secrets to explore

Cons:
- Leaving the server during a trace is kinda buggy
- You need to read a lot

[h1]Conclusions[/h1]
This is a nice hacking simulation game to spend your time with.

[h1]Should you buy this game?[/h1]
[b]Yes.[/b]
[i]If you like to play hacking simulation game, buy this. You might have to know a little bit about terminals though; you can actually play it without knowing it at all but it might give you a harder time, especially if you don't like to learn and read.[/i]

review_text_raw:
[b]Hacknet[/b] is a hacking simulation game. You are probably familiar with other games of the same genre, such as Uplink and the Hacker Evolution series. This game is, I dare to say, better than both of those, despite having some bugs.
If this review is too long for you, I suggest you to only read the first paragraph about the game's content and the final verdict at the end.

[h1]What is happening in the game:[/h1]
Fourteen days after Agent Bit's disappearance, a failsafe sequence was activated. You are one of the only people who can solve Bit's death. As you get more and more involved into the hacker community, you start unveiling a mystery and it's up to you to discover what was really behind Bit and the security system he created.

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[list]
    [*]After the success of Uplink, there had to be a game sooner or later that would try to improve what Uplink started. Hacknet not only achieves that, but takes it to the next level. The story alone is amazing and makes sure that you're not just repeating the same commands and actions over and over but gives it a meaning.
    [*]I have to say that the whole interface is working really nicely when it comes to clarity and effectiveness. You can do 90% of things both in the Display section and Terminal section, but they are both placed in the interface and I find it surprisingly effective. I use the Display section for figuring out what is going on and the Terminal section to execute commands.
    [*]You have a nice map on the bottom of the screen, that is showing all of the cyber locations you have visited already. As you get to connect to tons of computers, you would think that the map would be overcrowded, but this is not the case. I found the map really useful, despite it being almost completely covered.
    [*]There is no bouncing from servers as you remember from other hacking games. Instead, traces are lost if you simply disconnect. Even better is the way how the developers managed what happens if you get traced. Your computer (the virtual one, of course) activates a failsafe sequence. It tells you the IP of your ISP and your IP. You have to break into your ISP's server in a very limited amount of time and from there, reset your IP. This is a brilliant way to prevent accidental game overs and having to start all over again. Instead, you are provided with one more hard (and fun) challenge.
    [*]I really enjoy the soundtrack in this game. The song was written by a guy who also made the soundtrack for Hotline Miami. The music matches with the tension of your current illegal doings and really makes your heart beat faster. Amazing job.
    [*]The in-game hacking is based on actual UNIX commands, which is pretty cool. Still, don't expect to be a pro hacker when you finish this game. You would still be a few steps away, the first step being stopping playing hacking simulators instead of learning the real deal.
    [*]There is a ton of Easter Eggs in this game. A clicker game, hidden Steam keys and a lot more. It's really impressive how they manage to fit all sorts of things into this game. Also, you should read all of the IRC chat logs when you encounter them. They can be super funny (and useful).
    [*]I have cooperated with the developer in bug-related issues and I have to say that I really like the way that the developer interacts with the community. (Almost) all of the bugs I have encountered were fixed and I'm glad that they managed to bring the final release in a shape that they did.
    [*]Another interesting aspect of this game is puzzle solving. You have to think really hard to solve some of them and you even have to remember things from your previous missions, write things down and stuff like that.
    [*]If you don't like the user interface, you will encounter skins later in the game that you can download and make your virtual computer looks just the way you want.
    [*]The system requirements are low, which is great for old computers. However, there are some moments when FPS suddenly drops and gets to a normal level quickly.
    [*]$/€10 is a steal for a game of such quality. If you ever enjoyed hacking games, this should be the top game on your wishlist.
[/list]

[h1]Cons:[/h1]
[list]
    [*]Bugs. Many were fixed, but some are still present. The game-breaking ones are gone, however, so you should be fine.
    [*]This game should have a button to reset progress. I wanted to do that a couple of times but you can't really do that without browsing through folders and files.
[/list]

[h1]The final verdict:[/h1]
As a big fan of hacking games, I was very happy to be able to play Hacknet. The game is certainly made well and definitely recommend this game to you if you enjoy hacking games as well. The story is surprisingly good and adds an important part to the whole experience. The hacking really feels real and, even though that the commands are pretty much the same through the whole game, never feel repetitive.
This is, no doubt, the best hacking game ever released. Get it, and fast!

Greetings,
BirdCute

review_text_raw:
[b]DISCLAIMER: I was provided a press review copy for the purposes of documenting the game for PCGamingWiki, a publicly-editable technical wiki for games.[/b]

What would happen if you gamified the idea that you found a copy of an OS which was so dead-simple to use, anyone with basic computer and investigative skills could hack into [i]anything[/i]? You'd get Hacknet, an excellent hacking game designed to be the spiritual successor to Uplink. Slick graphics, a sliding difficulty designed to get you introduced to the game's mechancis one-by-one, and an in-the-background story which is surprisingly pointient and explores not only how insecure computers really are to a dedicated hacker, but the ramifications, both practical and mornal, of an OS designed to hack anything.

[b]TL;DR:[/b] It's a short, satisfying hacking game which, despite how complicated it seems at the outset, eases you into its mechanics, world, and story, and gives you the surprising, satisfying feeling of being both a master hacker and Sherlock Holmes at the same time.

[h1]Is this Uplink 2.0?[/h1]
For the mandatory "Is this Uplink 2.0" part of the review: no. This is [i]not[/i] the spiritual successor hardcore fans of Uplink have been looking for because:
[list]
[*] You use a 'real' computer with fixed specs, with HacknetOS running on top of it as a VM (Virtual Machine).
[*] The game is command-line based with some GUI helpers, such as an IP map, optional GUI-based system navigation, and a note app.
[*] You can only run computer-compromising apps via command-line.
[*] The game's story, despite being subtle, in the background, and without limitations (i.e. x number of connections before game over), drives the game, and your actions are ultimately in service of the story.
[/list]

If none of the above scared you off, then read on because this spiritual sequel is, in spite of the above, a worthy one IMO...
[h1]Gameplay[/h1]
As mentioned above, Hacknet uses its command-line for much of the hacking, with a few GUI helpers for those tasks too cumbersome to exclusively do in the GUI, like keeping track of all the known IPs and keeping notes. Despite this, there are only a few core commands, and are remarkably easy-to-remember with repeated use - and the game is [i]very[/i] careful to ensure you do - and often relate to what they do. For example, to crack an in-game computer's SSH port, run SSHcrack [insert port number here]. This is further helped by the addition of command auto-completion - something the game teaches you how to use very quickly. So, that SSHcrack command I just mentioned? All you really need to type in is SSH, press the TAB key, add the port number, and press the Enter key. Believe me - it makes your life a [i]lot[/i] easier.

The hacking itself is simple: connect to the target, probe the computer for weaknesses, then execute programs to exploit their weaknesses. Some computers require some preperatory work, such as computers with proxies effectively require you to use other computers you've compromised to attack them, while others might require you to find a piece of cracking software to open them up, bypass a firewall by running special software to solve its encryption, and so on. At first, it isn't so difficult - just run the apps, and watch the magic happen. Later on, you'll begin to regularly encounter computers which will attempt to passively hunt your computer down and force it to reboot - complete with a giant timer showing you the exact time to failure - requiring you to run multiple apps at once. Since your computer only has so much memory, you'll need to play Tetris with the apps, shutting down those you don't need and running the ones which bypass the easiest weaknessess. Beating the clock and compromising a computer with a second to spare is an accomplishment in an of itself which never gets old.

Another good thing is the game understands how counter-intuitive command-line use is for the average user, so through the use of an initial tutorial (which can be skipped once you know how to terminate it) and missions which slowly slide up in difficulty as they teach the basic mechanics, you'll eventually come to grips with the commands you need to hack. And once you do, it starts giving you missions which, combined with the clear, clever visuals (more on those later), allow you to feel like a master hacker in a way different from other hacking games because you'll often need to do something which most hacking games leave out entirely or towards the very end.

[b]You get to be Sherlock Holmes.[/b]

You see, because people, even those with good security sense, tend to forget or excuse security issues, they also tend to leave stuff on their computers, mobile devices, and e-mail accounts. IP addresses to secret files, administrator (admin) passwords for top-secret servers and their most private e-mails - you name it, they'll leave it. A key part of the gameplay is erasing anything in the system's logs indicating you were there so the authorities can't track your hacks back to you. In theory, this means deleting every log file before leaving the server; in practice, all you have to do in most cases is start deleting all the log files, disconnect from the server, wait for all the files to be deleted, then come back. This means that as long as the computer doesn't have a rotating admin password - and most don't - what should be down-to-the-wire hacks end up being trivial. Furthermore, any future accessing of the computer will be ignored - even if you never delete the logs after the first time.

I can't really touch on the story much as to do so would ruin the surprise and horror it provides late in the game. I can say, though, that the story, while simple, is quite sophisticated, as it explores through your actions just what kind of power HacknetOS gives those who own it in today's digital age, where everything - and I do mean [i]everything[/i] - is connected to the Internet and, thus, can be compromised, pried open, and tampered with.
[h1]Graphics[/h1]
The graphics in Hacknet are very minimalistic and clean, meaning you can see exactly what's what with minimal effort. There are also some optional, subtle effects which emulate a CRT computer monitor, adding to the realism. The standout graphics come from the apps, as they show you in fun and clever ways how they're progressing, whether it shows you punching through an SSH table with every section hacked turned green or beat out an SMTP mail server's sorting algorithm to force it to shut down and open up to you.
[h1]Additional Thoughts[/h1]
I really wish the game opened up towards the middle - it would've been fun exploring the world wide web, finding hidden sub-plots as you tear through the world's computers like tissue paper, as a reprieve from the short story. Speaking of the story, I also wish it were longer - the game's puzzles were clever and unique, and I so desperately wanted more content.

review_text_raw:
An interesting mix between Uplink and Street Hacker, for the price of ~10 USD is definitely worth checking out.

The game is pretty fun, some things require attention to detail and logical thinking, and the humor is pretty good!

However, the game launched with a very bad bug which might make your save useless: if you try to make two missions at a time, you won't be able to complete the first one. This can simply kill your save.
Also, even though the presentation is well done and the interface looks pretty, I don't see much advance over what other Hacking games did before (Uplink was released in 2001), so you really should approach this with caution. The biggest difference here is being able to use both a GUI and a Console - which is good news.

This doesn't detract from the enjoyment of the game, of course. But it does dissapoint if you expected anything more than that.

I haven't finished the game yet, due to the bug that probably broke my savegame. But about the plot: it's decently intriguing and will make you want to uncover all the secrets, as a hacking game should.

So even though I ended up pretty disappointed - it's 2015, yet there's little news here. Even Street Hacker, which is a decade old and terribly programmed, had deeper features; and Uplink had a more compelling gameplay and story - there's still some fun to be had and some jokes/moments actually made me laugh or smile. 
I do recommend waiting for a patch before playing it, though. So rush it on your own risk.

review_text_raw:
Cool Concept, But It Couldn’t Keep Me Hooked

Hacknet starts strong. The idea of diving into a terminal-based hacking sim with a mysterious narrative hook is instantly appealing, especially if you’re into cyberpunk aesthetics or want to feel like a digital detective. At first, typing out real commands and navigating the virtual systems feels immersive and fresh. But that feeling didn’t last long for me.

The main problem is how quickly the novelty wears off. After a couple of missions, the gameplay loop becomes repetitive — scan, probe, crack, read a few emails, rinse and repeat. There’s little variety or meaningful evolution in the mechanics. You’re not solving clever puzzles so much as going through the motions of the same routine over and over.

The story, while intriguing in concept, never really grabbed me. It’s told in fragments through logs and emails, but it lacks emotional weight or urgency. I never felt particularly invested in the characters or their motivations — and a lot of the writing just felt flat.

On top of that, there are some pacing issues. Some tasks feel tedious and drawn out, while others jump ahead abruptly. And if you’re not already familiar with basic command-line structure, the early learning curve can feel more frustrating than fun.

I really wanted to like Hacknet. It nails the aesthetic and tone, and I respect the ambition. But the shallow gameplay and underwhelming story made it feel more like a tech demo than a fully satisfying experience.

review_text_raw:
I’m not entirely sure what to think about this game. I feel like this game had the potential to be a lot more interesting than it turned out to be. I did have fun with this game and thought some of the missions were interesting. But, I can’t really figure out what this game is trying to be and I came away with the feeling that this game isn’t really finished. 

In terms of hacking and the operating system, it’s fairly weak and, at times, frustrating. The hacking programs you run are basically magic in terms of how powerful they are. They work on anything and require no modification based on the target. The challenge comes from managing your bizarre computer’s memory system and timing attacks to avoid the hollywood-style ‘tracing’. The simplified hacking mechanics aren’t a bad thing, I think. Real hacking elements would make the game extremely complicated, tedious, and boring. 

But, that aside, there are weird limitations on what you can do and what exists in the world. The operating system commands you run are unix-based, but quickly get frustrating to use for anyone familiar with *nix command lines. Autocompletion and wildcards are inconsistent (‘rm *’ works but not ‘rm file_*’). There is no cp (copy), mkdir, rmdir, rsync, or recursion-supported operations. There isn’t even a text editor of any kind, opting for a bizarre ‘replace’ to replace strings in a given file. This just causes more frustration than anything as folders become cluttered and basic OS actions can't be done.

As for the world, hacking into servers and snooping around is fun… to a point. You can read other people’s emails, deface websites, and steal files, which is fun! Then you realize that most of the files you discover are copy-pasted bash.org quotes or filler files which you can’t do anything with. Also, you’re strongly told early on to remove the log files you leave behind when hacking a server, but I’ve yet to find an instance where there are any consequences for not doing so outside of one mission. Finally, and probably my biggest problem, is that you’re pretty much the only active user on the entire internet. You’ll never accidentally encounter another hacker when breaking into a server and you’ll (with one exception) never find log files or evidence of dynamic activity from anyone else on the internet. The world is completely static, apart from a few scripted events. Maybe if there were random encounters or events with other hackers where both of you have the ability to hack each other and other servers, the world wouldn’t feel so static and empty and it would keep you on your toes a bit more. 

The investigation and puzzle aspects of the game are interesting. But, the large number of typos,  grammar mistakes (not sure if these two are intentional or not), and questionable writing can be distracting and confusing. That said, I still had fun. There are times where the missions can be very interesting and even disturbing. And, occasionally, there are times where you have to be clever to solve a puzzle or find a missing piece of information. But, those events are far and few in between. Most of the ‘contracts’ start to feel tedious pretty quickly.

I hate that there is no option inbetween the thumbs up and down, because I think the game is still fun. But, comparing how much I liked to how much I didn’t like, I have to give it a thumbs down. This game has great ideas, it just hasn’t fleshed them out enough.

review_text_raw:
[h1]What to expect if you're new to this game genre[/h1]
Hacknet is a new title in the otherwise stagnant, indie genre of hacking simulation games.
And a fresh breeze it is.

No doubt there is hardly any competition for this kind of quality.
Graphics are amazing, the hacking system introduced is quite good and consistent, it has gigantic potential for expansion that desperately needs to be used, and hopefully will. In it's current shape there might be little room for multiplayer gameplay, because of the game mechanics, but hopefully as the game gets finalized it will be implemented.

The puzzles you have to face are fun to solve and most of the time at medium or easy difficulty level.
Even though the game description provided on Steam might be a little misleading, as to non-holywood hacking style, or minimal hand-holding, the gameplay can be extremely exciting and satisfying.
The thrill of hacking, taking unauthorised control over websites, other web services, or user machines and mobile devices, identity theft or destruction, and constantly racing the trace clock are all very satisfying and will give you an addictive adrenaline rush.

Music is a very proper and enjoyable background for your virtual crimes, not quite something to remember.

The game has too high hardware requirements in my opinion. All in all it is a console based hacking game, and it is barely playable on i5, 4GB, Intel graphics HD4000 Lenovo laptop (12 fps max with too much typing lag!!!)

[h1]Finally the 'Uplink vs Hacknet'[/h1]
Many people look up to Hacknet in comparison to Uplink.
Based on my experiences with both titles If you did truly enjoy Uplink, You will be dazzled by Hacknet's modern design. Graphics are eyecandy.
The gameplay itself however, as compared to Uplink I have found to be short (if that can be said - I was unable to finish the game due to numerous bugs [despite 50+hrs in-game]), shallow and at many times unchallenging.
If you can bear with, well kinda outdated graphics and a little clumsy UI, I'd say Uplink offers far greater immersion, much more complex world to explore, more freedom, less hand holding.
Hardware upgrades covering several computer components to your machine, or even different, more upgradable machines (you can create them yourself or download one of many community created ones!!!!), software upgrades that all can be purchased are something you won't find in Hacknet, since finances have been taken out of the picture in the first place. Money earning, stock market participation and manipulation, and banking are all absent in Hacknet. So are LAN networks that pose a sublevel of gameplay in Uplink. Hacknet at this stage of developement also gives you the feeling of being the only web user out there, since only on rare story related events will you ever find logs left by anyone else on any servers (even the public services). Tracing other hackers or users is nearly non existent since the idea of connection bouncing has also been skipped so far. In my opinion, with similar development times of several years for both games, Uplink is a masterpiece bot technically and story-wise, compared to Hacknet.

[h1]Final words[/h1]
Whatever Hacknet is or will be, I'd say Uplink is worth playing, as the only other hacking game out there with some serious gameplay to this date.
If compatibility issues or the kinda-outdated-look are an obstacle for you playing Uplink, Hacknet will still be a very enjoyable and exciting experience, however I would strongly advise to wait with the purchase until numerous major bugs are addressed and more potential gets released from Hacknet, or you might be facing quite a frustrating struggle with what I can only call a beta version (at best) right now. I have also learned there is a free remake of Uplink to be found out there, I will let you find it yourself tho, since I'd stick with the original version by Introversion Software and support it's makers.
Keep track of Hacknet news and discussion on Steam for a stable version somewhen in the (hopefully) near future.

All in all it is a console based hacking game, and it is barely playable on i5, 4GB, Intel graphics HD4000 Lenovo laptop (12 fps max with too much typing lag!!!) [h1]Finally the 'Uplink vs Hacknet'[/h1] Many people look up to Hacknet in comparison to Uplink. Based on my experiences with both titles If you did truly enjoy Uplink, You will be dazzled by Hacknet's modern design. Graphics are eyecandy. The gameplay itself however, as compared to Uplink I have found to be short (if that can be said - I was unable to finish the game due to numerous bugs [despite 50+hrs in-game]), shallow and at many times unchallenging. If you can bear with, well kinda outdated graphics and a little clumsy UI, I'd say Uplink offers far greater immersion, much more complex world to explore, more freedom, less hand holding. Hardware upgrades covering several computer components to your machine, or even different, more upgradable machines (you can create them yourself or download one of many community created ones!!!!), software upgrades that all can be purchased are something you won't find in Hacknet, since finances have been taken out of the picture in the first place. Money earning, stock market participation and manipulation, and banking are all absent in Hacknet. So are LAN networks that pose a sublevel of gameplay in Uplink. Hacknet at this stage of developement also gives you the feeling of being the only web user out there, since only on rare story related events will you ever find logs left by anyone else on any servers (even the public services). Tracing other hackers or users is nearly non existent since the idea of connection bouncing has also been skipped so far. In my opinion, with similar development times of several years for both games, Uplink is a masterpiece bot technically and story-wise, compared to Hacknet. If compatibility issues or the kinda-outdated-look are an obstacle for you playing Uplink, Hacknet will still be a very enjoyable and exciting experience, however I would strongly advise to wait with the purchase until numerous major bugs are addressed and more potential gets released from Hacknet, or you might be facing quite a frustrating struggle with what I can only call a beta version (at best) right now. I have also learned there is a free remake of Uplink to be found out there, I will let you find it yourself tho, since I'd stick with the original version by Introversion Software and support it's makers. Keep track of Hacknet news and discussion on Steam for a stable version somewhen in the (hopefully) near future.

review_text_raw:
Wow, Hacknet is one immersive command line game.
You get to pick up the left overs of a now dead hacker, following in his footsteps, slowly taking on harder challenges and making a name for yourself.
Hacknet offers a tight narrative (which is completely text based) and enthralling 'hacking'

Pros:
 - presentation. I know a lot of people will be turned off by a CL interface game. but heck (huehue), it's beautiful, intuitive and well designed. plus you can download more UIs from servers and people you hacked
 - gameplay. it's relatively easy, requiring (so far, I'm roughly 4 hours into the game) simple management skills, a keen eye and some reading and prioritizing. the hacking is served well, not letting you button mash, but rather focused on the finer points such as: reading emails for usernames and passwords, changing websites headers into vulgarities, finding the right tools and balance, covering your tracks.
     a lot of the gameplay is indeed done over a command line interface, which, exactly, means you type out what you wanna do. there's helps, and little tools making it a lot easier than real life hacking could ever be.
- Story. it's a pretty cool mix of paranoia, technology and a weird form of justice. no one talks, no fancy cutscenes. it's all in your head, buddy
 - immersion. yeah, the computers you hack are rather empty, but what is on there is hilarious and often gives small hints to connections between the hackers you 'meet' (I think, at least
 - music. absolutely perfect. 

Cons:
 - uhm, let me think ... hmmm ... no, it is exactly what it says it is. and then some

Verdict:

You like hacking/hacking movies or just recently discovered Mr Robot or the deep web?
Well, come on in. this is a perfect supplement to your diet.
Hacknet is pretty (for CL standards :D as I work in IT I actually find it gorgeous), fun and fast paced. It will test your patience, but mostly your ability to read and type properly.
But nothing is keeping it from delivering the best hacker game since Uplink, if not even a tick better.
And it is totally worth the price tag

review_text_raw:
[b]Hacknet[/b] is a hacking simulation game. You are probably familiar with other games of the same genre, such as Uplink and the Hacker Evolution series. This game is, I dare to say, better than both of those, despite having some bugs.
If this review is too long for you, I suggest you to only read the first paragraph about the game's content and the final verdict at the end.

[h1] What is happening in the game: [/h1]
Fourteen days after Agent Bit's disappearance, a failsafe sequence was activated. You are one of the only people who can solve Bit's death. As you get more and more involved into the hacker community, you start unveiling a mystery and it's up to you to discover what was really behind Bit and the security system he created.

[h1]Pros:[/h1]
[list]
[*]After the success of Uplink, there had to be a game sooner or later that would try to improve what Uplink started. Hacknet not only achieves that, but takes it to the next level. The story alone is amazing and makes sure that you're not just repeating the same commands and actions over and over but gives it a meaning.
[*]I have to say that the whole interface is working really nicely when it comes to clarity and effectiveness. You can do 90% of things both in the Display section and Terminal section, but they are both placed in the interface and I find it surprisingly effective. I use the Display section for figuring out what is going on and the Terminal section to execute commands.
[*]You have a nice map on the bottom of the screen, that is showing all of the cyber locations you have visited already. As you get to connect to tons of computers, you would think that the map would be overcrowded, but this is not the case. I found the map really useful, despite it being almost completely covered.
[*]There is no bouncing from servers as you remember from other hacking games. Instead, traces are lost if you simply disconnect. Even better is the way how the developers managed what happens if you get traced. Your computer (the virtual one, of course) activates a failsafe sequence. It tells you the IP of your ISP and your IP. You have to break into your ISP's server in a very limited amount of time and from there, reset your IP. This is a brilliant way to prevent accidental game overs and having to start all over again. Instead, you are provided with one more hard (and fun) challenge.
[*]I really enjoy the soundtrack in this game. The song was written by a guy who also made the soundtrack for Hotline Miami. The music matches with the tension of your current illegal doings and really makes your heart beat faster. Amazing job.
[*]The in-game hacking is based on actual UNIX commands, which is pretty cool. Still, don't expect to be a pro hacker when you finish this game. You would still be a few steps away, the first step being stopping playing hacking simulators instead of learning the real deal.
[*]There is a ton of Easter Eggs in this game. A clicker game, hidden Steam keys and a lot more. [*]It's really impressive how they manage to fit all sorts of things into this game. Also, you should read all of the IRC chat logs when you encounter them. They can be super funny (and useful).
[*]I have cooperated with the developer in bug-related issues and I have to say that I really like the way that the developer interacts with the community. (Almost) all of the bugs I have encountered were fixed and I'm glad that they managed to bring the final release in a shape that they did.
[*]Another interesting aspect of this game is puzzle solving. You have to think really hard to solve some of them and you even have to remember things from your previous missions, write things down and stuff like that.
[*]If you don't like the user interface, you will encounter skins later in the game that you can download and make your virtual computer looks just the way you want.
[*]The system requirements are low, which is great for old computers. However, there are some moments when FPS suddenly drops and gets to a normal level quickly.
[*]$/€10 is a steal for a game of such quality. If you ever enjoyed hacking games, this should be the top game on your wishlist.

[h1]Cons:[/h1]
Bugs. Many were fixed, but some are still present. The game-breaking ones are gone, however, so you should be fine.
This game should have a button to reset progress. I wanted to do that a couple of times but you can't really do that without browsing through folders and files.

[h1]The final verdict:[/h1]
As a big fan of hacking games, I was very happy to be able to play Hacknet. The game is certainly made well and definitely recommend this game to you if you enjoy hacking games as well. The story is surprisingly good and adds an important part to the whole experience. The hacking really feels real and, even though that the commands are pretty much the same through the whole game, never feel repetitive.
This is, no doubt, the best hacking game ever released. Get it, and fast!

This was Kedeajan,
Have fun!

review_text_raw:
[h1] Many will claim that this is like playing the next version of Uplink since it is the most realistic hacking type game since Uplink was released. A very unique genre I think with very few games making a significant mark. I cannot claim to have played that classic so I will have to describe this entertaining game called Hacknet without any past comparisons. I will say that the reason it is compared though is because it takes the hacking seriously and isn't just some casual hacking game for the masses. [/h1]

Hacknet has almost no graphics (Maybe about 5 image files in the entire game), it has no video. It is only you looking at a computer screen full of numbers and files. You are a hacker, not Rambo, or James Bond, or Batman. You don't shoot at criminals and punch clowns in the face to save the day. You are a hacker that has found yourself in the middle of some hacking factions that may have stumbled into something big. You get some simple clues at the start that something is going on, but as you delve deeper into the hacking world, get recruited by more skillful hacking groups, and find more mysterious actions going on in your hacking exploits you will get asked to help find out what happened to a popular hacker that has gone missing. Just like everything in the hacking community, all useful information is hidden on systems which need to be hacked into. While looking for that information you will uncover many more secrets as you figure out exactly what happened. A final ending that could be considered a "shock". Very intriguing storyline and way to tell a story all through computer documents, e-mails, IRC chats, etc.

While the tutorials, and the game itself is friendly to those who have no experience entering command lines, or hacking at all, it may not exactly be for the most casual of gamers. If you are a VERY slow typist you may have some issues when it comes to hacking into computers here in the time frames that are allowed. They have made it easier for you by allowing you to hit "TAB" in certain places to have the game auto-complete command lines if there is nothing else that has the exact same characters and you are in the proper place to do so, however. It absolutely helps to have some typing speed, or at least the knowledge of where all the keys on the keyboard are without having to search them out all the time though. You will have issues if you are THAT slow.

You are tasked with finding various tools to run .exe files allowing you to open up ports on the computers you hack before running a PortHack program to get access to its files. Some computers early on are very easy to hack with only having to open 1-2 ports, but as you find more tools you may have to open as many as 5 ports, break through a firewall, and get through a proxy all on the same PC while avoiding a tracer too! So it becomes a bit quicker later on where you must know the commands and how to crack the security of various systems as the game progresses while fighting a clock too. You should pick up these skills as you play, but the knowledge of how to access certain databases will require a bit more thought at times. This is where the game adds a bit of strategy and puzzling into the mix. You need to think about what you are trying to do, search through maybe several other computers not just tools, but possibly passwords to OTHER computers, and even find ways to crack encrypted files! So it isn't always completely straightforward with the game holding your hand to get what you need. You will absolutely need to think somewhat critically here to reach your goals. IT is very refreshing to find a game that doesn't just offer you solutions on a silver platter and challenges you to figure things out yourself. It is quite rewarding in some cases to find a solution after thinking all your options through. Sometimes you can even find solutions to future problems by just HACKING into things you aren't even supposed to be working on for no other reason than because you felt like it.

Hacknet had a few bugs when I got it at release, but it appears that most have been taken care of. I finished the game, but I had a quest that didn't trigger properly so I had to hack my way around into other things to find the info I needed to proceed. Something that really wasn't that big a deal because it felt like I was actually doing something I figured out myself to get around a problem. The triggers have been patched now though as far as I know. Other than that nothing I ran into.

Hacknet does make you feel like a hacker if you have never done any hacking before in your life. It does use real world terminology and command lines to satisfy those that have in the past too so it isn't just for the hacker n00bs out there. The fast paced and tech-y music playing in the background was designed to make you feel like you are hacking systems as a hero in a movie. Punching in commands as fast you can can before getting caught is definitely helped by the pace of the music playing while you are trying to look into the dirty secrets of every computer you hack into.

I found Hacknet to be a fantastic feeling of hacking and mystery solving. While you may feel that the middle gets a little bit repetitive when it comes to the hacking, it does usually change up enough in what you need to use to keep the pacing OK. Usually what you find in the files, and of course the ending was payoff enough to continue through if you start to feel like you are staring at a flashing screen too long. I absolutely would not recommend this game to a casual gamer at all. Unlike say a point and click adventure, the puzzles you solve here will require quick thinking and quick fingers at times. Most players will be fine with this, but this is a game that require MUCH more activity on the keyboard than it does with a mouse. So you are typing commands for what you need to do in, and not using a mouse to solve puzzles as much. If you don't read the help files, the tutorial, and look at the academic databases in the game you will not be able to figure things out. If you want a brainless game this one is not for you.

The game has trading cards of course and Steam Achievements, which should be fairly easy to 100% if you can get through the game. This game should take you anywhere from 5-10 hours. More if you look around some and find every secret I suspect.

NOTE: Something I didn't talk about, because I am unsure what it consists of, is that Hacknet will be releasing a patch at some point that includes not just Steam Workshop to add more player made "questing", but it will also have Multiplayer! Like I said I don't know much about those aspects, but they are definitely coming. MP was in the game before Steam so it already exists, but the developers didn't feel it was working well enough yet to release with the Steam release. They wanted to stamp out any single player bugs first before bringing in these other features.

You are tasked with finding various tools to run .exe files allowing you to open up ports on the computers you hack before running a PortHack program to get access to its files. Some computers early on are very easy to hack with only having to open 1-2 ports, but as you find more tools you may have to open as many as 5 ports, break through a firewall, and get through a proxy all on the same PC while avoiding a tracer too! So it becomes a bit quicker later on where you must know the commands and how to crack the security of various systems as the game progresses while fighting a clock too. You should pick up these skills as you play, but the knowledge of how to access certain databases will require a bit more thought at times. This is where the game adds a bit of strategy and puzzling into the mix. You need to think about what you are trying to do, search through maybe several other computers not just tools, but possibly passwords to OTHER computers, and even find ways to crack encrypted files! So it isn't always completely straightforward with the game holding your hand to get what you need. You will absolutely need to think somewhat critically here to reach your goals. IT is very refreshing to find a game that doesn't just offer you solutions on a silver platter and challenges you to figure things out yourself. It is quite rewarding in some cases to find a solution after thinking all your options through. Sometimes you can even find solutions to future problems by just HACKING into things you aren't even supposed to be working on for no other reason than because you felt like it. Hacknet had a few bugs when I got it at release, but it appears that most have been taken care of. I finished the game, but I had a quest that didn't trigger properly so I had to hack my way around into other things to find the info I needed to proceed. Something that really wasn't that big a deal because it felt like I was actually doing something I figured out myself to get around a problem. The triggers have been patched now though as far as I know. Other than that nothing I ran into. Hacknet does make you feel like a hacker if you have never done any hacking before in your life. It does use real world terminology and command lines to satisfy those that have in the past too so it isn't just for the hacker n00bs out there. The fast paced and tech-y music playing in the background was designed to make you feel like you are hacking systems as a hero in a movie. Punching in commands as fast you can can before getting caught is definitely helped by the pace of the music playing while you are trying to look into the dirty secrets of every computer you hack into. I found Hacknet to be a fantastic feeling of hacking and mystery solving. While you may feel that the middle gets a little bit repetitive when it comes to the hacking, it does usually change up enough in what you need to use to keep the pacing OK. Usually what you find in the files, and of course the ending was payoff enough to continue through if you start to feel like you are staring at a flashing screen too long. I absolutely would not recommend this game to a casual gamer at all. Unlike say a point and click adventure, the puzzles you solve here will require quick thinking and quick fingers at times. Most players will be fine with this, but this is a game that require MUCH more activity on the keyboard than it does with a mouse. So you are typing commands for what you need to do in, and not using a mouse to solve puzzles as much. If you don't read the help files, the tutorial, and look at the academic databases in the game you will not be able to figure things out. If you want a brainless game this one is not for you. The game has trading cards of course and Steam Achievements, which should be fairly easy to 100% if you can get through the game. This game should take you anywhere from 5-10 hours. More if you look around some and find every secret I suspect. NOTE: Something I didn't talk about, because I am unsure what it consists of, is that Hacknet will be releasing a patch at some point that includes not just Steam Workshop to add more player made "questing", but it will also have Multiplayer! Like I said I don't know much about those aspects, but they are definitely coming. MP was in the game before Steam so it already exists, but the developers didn't feel it was working well enough yet to release with the Steam release. They wanted to stamp out any single player bugs first before bringing in these other features.

review_text_raw:
1. You can't finish all contracts. At some point the game will just tell you "You're good enough for more difficult tasks" and a main quest will trigger, blocking you from accepting new quests. You can never go back and you can't do them after the final mission.

2. You can't create files or directories. Organizing your downloaded files is annoying because you can only use the pre-defined ones. In one contract you're supposed to forge a file, and that works by downloading a file and editing the copy...

3. You can't remove directories. There's almost never a need to do so, but when you need to remove the contents from a directory with multiple subdirectories, you need to access each subdir individually and remove the contents.

4. Autocomplete doesn't add a whitespace after the autocompleteted word. Confusing as hell for a regular terminal user.

5. The final mission consists of multiple phases, which each one explaining your next goal. In phase 3 you're supposed to send a password but you aren't told so. I just used the password I found to login and continued my quest. After a while I got stuck, and after more than an hour I finally looked into a walkthrough - and learnt that I needed to send the password instead of entering it, and that had already solved the final mission by myself over an hour ago. At least I could just click the "complete quest" button 4 times in a row to trigger the ending.

6. The gameplay is quite repetetive. Connect to a server, open the closed ports (which always works the same, for all of them), find the file you need. There are only 2 missions that go beyond that and actually force you to think: The final mission, and the mission before. That doesn't really speak for the game.

7. The map is just plain awful. It's cluttered with nodes from earlier contracts which you never need to connect to anymore. Literally hardest part of the game is finding the correct node on the map.

8. Secrets. Don't get me wrong, secrets are great. But I looked into a guide after finishing the game, and some secrets didn't trigger for me although I definitely satisfied their conditions. So maybe I shouldn't have written "Secrets", but "Bugs". Furthermore, some secrets get you hyped, and when you finally solve their puzzle, you get... a digital clock that even uses up your RAM?

9. Alt+Tab closes the game.

I completed the game in a single session. It was kinda fun, although way too easy. But damn, some of the issues I just mentioned are pissing me off and I'm not going to play the DLC or any user-created mod.

Great idea - terrible execution. For the whole duration of the game you perform same actions again, again and again. And again. Oh, and AGAIN. The totally optional Clicker mini-game and tutorial are the best and most memorable parts of it, and that's saying something.

All of this game's content can be listed as follows:
do {

*check your email, get contract details*
probe
-- Oh, heck, a proxy again.
connect xxx.xxx.xxx.xxx
shell
connect sss.sss.sss.sss
connect yyy.yyy.yyy.yyy
shell
connect sss.sss.sss.sss
connect zzz.zzz.zzz.zzz
shell
connect sss.sss.sss.sss
connect... -- nah, that's probably enough, I still need to "hack" that firewall.
*overloading proxy*
analyze
analyze
analyze
analyze
analyze
*Proxy bypassed*
analyze
analyze
analyze
analyze
solve XXXXXXX
WebServerWorm 80
SMTPoverflow 25
FTPbounce 21
SSHcrack 22
*waiting until the end of it*
porthack
*waiting again*
-- Finally.
*doing same repeatative stuff on the hacked machine, clear logs, disconnect*

} while true;

And that's about it. You don't even have to think. At all. More than that, you actually CAN'T think to improve something in your game. Everything you do here is just following instructions like a machine. Bypass Propxy, solve Firewall, open ports, hack ports, get data, clear logs, disconnect, rinse and repeat. Since I didn't actually finish the game, I guess there will be more "hacking tools" introduced, but it won't change anything. The core of the game stays the same - just mindless repetition. This has nothing to do with actual cybersecurity business.

The moral side of some contracts is also questionable, to say the least. They want you to:
- get a private medical card of a person (for the sake of curiosity of some idiot forum-dweller);
- forge a degree for some "ally guy" of the (illegal) group you're working for.
- bring the secret [strike]KFC[/strike]CFC spice recepie out to the public, just, you know, for fun;
And that's only what I've encountered so far.

Some of the more "officially looking" contracts also make little sense. Like the one given to you by a high school administration, where you need to get IT admin password, so the administration can personally investigate a suspicion of IT department sharing student's emails data with outsiders (presumably, student's parents). It's so ridiculously stupid it could actually be another (one of many) dev's attempt at humour.


A word of advice:
If you suddenly became interested in all this "terminal net graph hacker cool" thing, just get VMWare\Oracle, download some Linux distros and build your own virtual network to play with. Way more fun, inherently legal and educative way of spending hours upon hours of your time typing stuff in CLI.

I picked this game up after a friend sent me a link from the Humble Bundle store to obtain a copy for free. Being free, I thought, "why not?" and picked it up. Boy, was I not disappointed. This was one neat game.

+Pros+
+ Quick game play
+ Simplistic, but not too much so
+ Tells a good story
+ Can run on a low spec computer
+ Decent Soundtrack

-Cons-
- Short story line (helped by the DLC that actually is a decent DLC)
- Story can be buried, but can be found with some digging
- Messy map overlay (Fixed by DLC, but still.)
- May have to use guide to get past one part [spoiler] Once Naix deletes your x-system [/spoiler] if you have no clue what's going on
- Game play depends on how fast you can get commands out, for slower typers, this may be a hindrance to game play

For being a fake hacking game, it still tests you and encourages you to mess up- there's a way to fix mistakes. While I only put perhaps 6 hours (2.5 online to get achievements) in to beat the game, the time differs per person depending on how much reading you do, and how fast you can type. The story starts off good, and you can easily forget what you were supposed to be doing once you complete some of the major tasks- but the game pulls you back into the main story line after you've built up your hacking tools and you have gained familiarity of the game's mechanics. For how simplistic it may seem, it easily sucks you into that world and allows you to be the hacker. You are controlling Hacknet. Good luck.

review_text_raw:
HACKNET - 7/10

Quick Review: A "hacking simulator" with gameplay akin to getting your first DOS system up and running, Hacknets weak story doesn't hold back the interesting and ever expanding gameplay.

Story
------
You, an amateur hacker, are contacted by someone named "Bit", who gives you an extra tool to add to your hacking repertoire and from there the expansive world is open to you. Using your new found tools, you become a part of something greater, helping (obviously shady) people with your hacking skills while trying to figure out just what the hell the Hacknet really is, and it might be more dangerous than you thought...

Overall, unfortunately the story is the weakest point. Everything is told through text in the game and the story really only starts to open up and become explained by the end but by that time you're more than likely burnt out from your constant reading. Most of the game has you completing irrelevant odd jobs for obvious scum with little relevance to the story, which is why the story is the weakest part.

Gameplay
-----------
Gameplay of Hacknet involves 2 things: typing and hacking. Your UI is a command window with a display of the target computer in the center, all the devices you have access to at the bottom and the command console on the right. Basic gameplay goes like this: Select a PC you want to hack, you "probe" it (by typing "probe") which will display a list of security measures. You then type whatever relevant command you need for the security measure (theres about 6 different types and you'll get the tools required as you progress through the game), wait a bit for it to be hacked, than do whatever it is the quest needs you to do; either copy a file to your system, delete a file, edit a file, find an ip address and send it to the client etc. The entire game revolves around typing commands and clicking files.

I do think the gameplay is fun however, it has to be for me to give it a 7/10. By the time you get the hang of your newly introduced command, you'll learn yet another and another until you get near the end. There is alot you can do and quite alot of secrets to find as you make your way through the story. The gameplay at it's core is simple but it takes a while to memorise all the power you have.

Design
-------
The UI for the game is great, and the gameplay experience really makes you feel like H4CK3RM@NZ.  You get access to different coloured themes as you progress, and alot of the files you can find on the computers are quite hilarious. The soundtrack is a banger too, and the end of the game features some of the best final music i've ever heard.

Problems
----------
It's a simple game, so it has simple problems. Alot of the text files you find on computers are just copy pasted across many devices, filling them up so you spend more time browsing through them than needed. There was a bit too much waiting involved when it came to hacking and required almost 0 thought, you simply type the command for whatever hacking tool you need and the number that corresponds with it, then you wait. The biggest problem I have is that as you get further and further in the game, the amount of devices you can access starts to clutter your device map. Because devices are represented as circles with no names, I spent ages hovering over 30+ circles trying to find what computer I was looking for, and they end up overlapping sometimes too. This sometimes made me have to re-hack into a previous computer to find the IP for the computer I wanted to hack into even if I already had it available, simply because it was impossible to find on my device map.

Achievements
---------------
The achievements are....relatively easy and can be gotten in 1 playthrough but you need to know what to do without the game telling you. You need to discover quite a few secrets and go out of your way to get alot of the achievements but there isn't an enormous amount of content in the game so as long as you try and explore everything you'll probably get them.

Summary
----------
A super unique experience and nothing like i've ever played. The banging soundtrack and addictive gameplay makes me easily recommend this, but only if you can overlook it's numerous, but not awful problems.

Also I can't stress enough the end of the game. It's seriously, SERIOUSLY amazing and worth playing just to experience it. Everything about it is great and the song that plays alongside it couldn't have been more perfect...for anything.

review_text_raw:
Many will claim that this is like playing the next version of Uplink since it is the most realistic hacking type game since Uplink was released. A very cult genre I think with very few games making a significant mark. I cannot claim to have played that classic so I will have to describe this entertaining game called Hacknet without any past comparisons. I will say that the reason it is compared though is because it takes the hacking seriously and isn't just some casual hacking game for the masses. 

Hacknet has almost no graphics (Maybe about 5 image files in the entire game), it has no video. It is only you looking at a computer screen full of numbers and files. You are a hacker, not Rambo, or James Bond, or Batman. You don't shoot at criminals and punch clowns in the face to save the day. You are a hacker that has found yourself in the middle of some hacking factions that may have stumbled into something big. You get some simple clues at the start that something is going on, but as you delve deeper into the hacking world, get recruited by more skillful hacking groups, and find more mysterious actions going on in your hacking exploits you will get asked to help find out what happened to a popular hacker that has gone missing. Just like everything in the hacking community, all useful information is hidden on systems which need to be hacked into. While looking for that information you will uncover many more secrets as you figure out exactly what happened. A final ending that could be considered a "shock". Very intriguing storyline and way to tell a story all through computer documents, e-mails, IRC chats, etc. 

While the tutorials, and the game itself is friendly to those who have no experience entering command lines, or hacking at all, it may not exactly be for the most casual of gamers. If you are a VERY slow typist you may have some issues when it comes to hacking into computers here in the time frames that are allowed. They have made it easier for you by allowing you to hit "TAB" in certain places to have the game auto-complete command lines if there is nothing else that has the exact same characters and you are in the proper place to do so, however. It absolutely helps to have some typing speed, or at least the knowledge of where all the keys on the keyboard are without having to search them out all the time though. You will have issues if you are THAT slow.  

You are tasked with finding various tools to run .exe files allowing you to open up ports on the computers you hack before running a PortHack program to get access to its files. Some computers early on are very easy to hack with only having to open 1-2 ports, but as you find more tools you may have to open as many as 5 ports, break through a firewall, and get through a proxy all on the same PC while avoiding a tracer too! So it becomes a bit quicker later on where you must know the commands and how to crack the security of various systems as the game progresses while fighting a clock too. You should pick up these skills as you play, but the knowledge of how to access certain databases will require a bit more thought at times. This is where the game adds a bit of strategy and puzzling into the mix. You need to think about what you are trying to do, search through maybe several other computers not just tools, but possibly passwords to OTHER computers, and even find ways to crack encrypted files! So it isn't always completely straightforward with the game holding your hand to get what you need. You will absolutely need to think somewhat critically here to reach your goals. IT is very refreshing to find a game that doesn't just offer you solutions on a silver platter and challenges you to figure things out yourself. It is quite rewarding in some cases to find a solution after thinking all your options through. Sometimes you can even find solutions to future problems by just HACKING into things you aren't even supposed to be working on for no other reason than because you felt like it. 

Hacknet had a few bugs when I got it at release, but it appears that most have been taken care of. I finished the game, but I had a quest that didn't trigger properly so I had to hack my way around into other things to find the info I needed to proceed. Something that really wasn't that big a deal because it felt like I was actually doing something I figured out myself to get around a problem. The triggers have been patched now though as far as I know. Other than that nothing I ran into. 

Hacknet does make you feel like a hacker if you have never done any hacking before in your life. It does use real world terminology and command lines to satisfy those that have in the past too so it isn't just for the hacker n00bs out there. The fast paced and tech-y music playing in the background was designed to make you feel like you are hacking systems as a hero in a movie. Punching in commands as fast you can can before getting caught is definitely helped by the pace of the music playing while you are trying to look into the dirty secrets of every computer you hack into. 

I found Hacknet to be a fantastic feeling of hacking and mystery solving. While you may feel that the middle gets a little bit repetitive when it comes to the hacking, it does usually change up enough in what you need to use to keep the pacing OK. Usually what you find in the files, and of course the ending was payoff enough to continue through if you start to feel like you are staring at a flashing screen too long. I absolutely would not recommend this game to a casual gamer at all. Unlike say a point and click adventure, the puzzles you solve here will require quick thinking and quick fingers at times. Most players will be fine with this, but this is a game that require MUCH more activity on the keyboard than it does with a mouse. So you are typing commands for what you need to do in, and not using a mouse to solve puzzles as much. If you don't read the help files, the tutorial, and look at the academic databases in the game you will not be able to figure things out. If you want a brainless game this one is not for you.

The game has trading cards of course and Steam Achievements, which should be fairly easy to 100% if you can get through the game. This game should take you anywhere from 5-10 hours. More if you look ar ound some and find every secret I suspect.

NOTE: Something I didn't talk about, because I am unsure what it consists of, is that Hacknet will be releasing a patch at some point that includes not just Steam Workshop to add more player made "questing", but it will also have Multiplayer! Like I said I don't know much about those aspects, but they are definitely coming. MP was in the game before Steam so it already exists, but the developers didn't feel it was working well enough yet to release with the Steam release. They wanted to stamp out any single player bugs first before bringing in these other features.

review_text_raw:
I feel slightly bad giving this game a negative review given that I enjoyed most of the time I spent playing it, but I honestly can't recommend it.

The positives are more than adequately covered in other reviews, but for completeness: It does a solid job of recreating the Hollywood hacker fantasy, with hacks and counter-hacks, proxies, firewalls, trace countdowns, and all that good stuff. The story is nicely paced, with plenty of humour and knowing pop-culture references as you move from small-time nuisance hacks to big-time corporate takedowns. And there is a mildly satisfying payoff when you figure out the occasional less-than-straightforward mission or discover a new mechanic.

Therein lies one of the major problems for me, though. For the most part the missions are fairly routine and don't really require any genuine creativity or problem-solving. You are pretty much handed the tools you need as you need them, and for each obstacle you need to overcome there will be a single tool for the job. As an example: the procedure for bypassing a firewall is to repeatedly type the 'analyze' command until you get the solution, and then to type in that solution - once you have done that once, it is entirely routine. I rarely felt clever solving the missions, and for a game like this I consider that a major failing.

As another reviewer pointed out, there are also elements of the game that seem to be either completely superficial or just unfinished. The best example is the scrubbing of logs, which is quite laborious, but presented at the beginning of the game as a vital measure to cover your tracks. So, the player diligently does so, until inevitably one time they forget, and then DUN DUN DUN...nothing. Apparently this feature is better implemented in the DLC extensions, but I didn't get that far.

Finally, the aspect of the game that ultimately ruined it for me: it is possible to irrevocably break your save game and have no way to recover. If you accidentally delete a file that is mission-critical to the main storyline, and don't notice until the next auto-save (or you save the game yourself), it's game over. This happened to me at about the 4.5 hour mark, and while it certainly wouldn't have taken me that long to get back to the same point from scratch, the game just doesn't work as a rogue-like - I would be going through exactly the same fiddly steps to complete exactly the same routine missions, and I just couldn't face it.

If you want to play a hacking game with a similar aesthetic but some genuine code-based problem-solving, I'd strongly recommend EXAPUNKS, or for an absolutely brilliant command-prompt-based-rogue-like try Duskers.

review_text_raw:
[+] Soundtrack
[+] User Interface

[-] Plot
[-] World design and interaction

I bought this game mainly for its soundtrack, then because I'm a terminal guy myself and I love typing commands.
From this standpoint the game is beautiful: hastily keyboard mashing while listening to Gallego's killer tracks was awesome, not even mentioning the time when Carpenter Brut took over...

This game perfectly sets the mood for an awesome experience, with its music, its terminals and pseudo-graphical GUIs... but then falls short story-side.

[b]The plot is dull, linear and somewhat predictable.[/b]
You only have one bifurcation of the storyline that's even non-obvious to unlock. It gives you access to some more interesting missions, a new faction, and let you see a dark corner of the in-game Internet; but then it merges back into the main path in an abrupt way, as meaningless as it could get.
Yes, there are some interesting easter eggs and strange computer systems, but nothing that makes you want to explore on your own all that much.
There's only, like, [i]one[/i] moral choice, and it's not even part of the main quest.

[b]Whatever you do, whoever you damage, there's no consequence. The world simply doesn't react.[/b]
No cops backtracing you, no factions you can anger, no reputation system: you're part of the Good Guys from start to finish; you can screw up all the machines you want, you are The Savior and no one will change that.
Heck, you can even fail hacks and, apart from a panicking minigame to atone, no officer nor corporate killer will ever knock on your door.
You're simply bounced from a Good faction to another, without any chance to express your will. Just keep on hacking. Don't even bother to cover up your footprints. Logs are useless.

In the end, yes you can buy it, sure, but don't expect much except aesthetics.


[TECHNICAL NOTE]
The in-game console is backed by your native OS, and everything is deeply woven with its runtime.
Yes, you read it right.
That means two things:
[list]
    [*] if some of your game files break, you can be welcomed by an OS error printed on the console;
    [*] while this game runs on both Windows and Linux and has cloud sync, the save files are [b]not[/b] cross-platform; I suspect it has to do with different text encodings (save files are simple XMLs), and you need a repair tool you can find on the forums in order to convert them.
[/list]
Yeah, that wasn't nice.

Hacknet is an immersive, terminal-based hacking simulator for PC. Dive down a rabbit hoIe as you follow the instructions of a recently deceased hacker, whose death may not have been the accident the media reports. Using old school command prompts and real hacking processes, you’ll solve the mystery with minimal hand-holding and a rich world full of secrets to explore.

Bit, a hacker responsible for creating the most invasive security system on the planet, is dead. When he fails to reconnect to his system for 14 days, his failsafe kicks in, sending instructions in automated emails to a lone user. As that user, it’s up to you to unravel the mystery and ensure that Hacknet-OS doesn't fall into the wrong hands.

Exploring the volatile nature of personal privacy, the prevalence of corporate greed, and the hidden powers of hackers on the internet, Hacknet delivers a true hacking simulation, while offering a support system that allows total beginners get a grasp of the real-world applications and commands found throughout the game.

review_text_raw:
[b][h1]I almost wanted to write this as a negative review.[/h1][/b]
However, on balance, I switched the direction of that thumb.

Full disclosure: I am a professional sysadmin, and I Tux and I are old buddies. He didn't like me at first, but I pulled his source and patched it, and now he [b]loves[/b] me. 

[h1] First the things that drove me up the wall...[/h1]

Mostly, it was the [b]almost[/b] unix commands, like 'RM *' instead of 'rm -r -f' and things like supporting tab completion and wildcards but [i]not[/i] partial names [i]with[/i] wildcards. I can't tell you how many times muscle memory had me type 'RM @32[Tab]*' to delete all logs that began with @3213 - but this does [i]not[/i] work in-game. You either delete everything, or have to type in each file one at a time. Fortunately, this ultimately proved irrelevant after I later discovered all other in-game admins use their keyboards only as a protective drool mat for their desks (more on that below.)

Also, the fact that you could just RM * and expect that the sysadmin on the system wouldnot find it suspicious at all that the system lacks logs of any kind for a whole time perod, and the last log is a x.x.x.x disconnected with no matching 'connected' message. Nope. Nothing suspicious there.

Almost makes me ashamed of wearing a white hat in real life. 

[h1]Kudos to the devs to for trying to acquaint us with RFC1700, but...[/h1]

What I found silly and pointless was to use real port numbers that you'd exepct to see in real life servers (22 for ssh, etc) but making you type in the port numbers for your magic 'sploit to work against (where there is never any deviation [i][b]ever[/b][/i] from the standard) is just silly as well.

[i]Note: I guess the IANA in-game must have been OK with that company creating the protocol that uses port 104, as that is in the range of ports they control assignments for... Just sayin' [/i]

I would assume a hacker as talented as 'bit' that could write a magic rootkit could figure out that if I didn't provide a port number for an SSH exploit, that it should just assume something as reasonable as, oh... assuming that the ssh daemon is running on port 22 like every. single. system. in the game's universe.

[h1]Word to the devs: It's either 'magic' hacking, or it's realistic. Pick your direction and don't try to do both at once.[/h1]

I guess my complaints kind of revolved around the fence sitting. Why go to all that trouble to get many technical details right, but still use hacking tools that so advanced as to appear 'magic' but at the same time retarded in so many easily fixed ways.

They even showed enough 'nix savvy to use tools like ps and kill mostly accurately and to cleverly make 'nmap' the command to trigger a scan for listening ports.
