review_text_raw:
Yes, yes, yes, more of this please.

Where are all the DLCs? We need more! There's only one DLC, really?!

Great game with a good story and in-game terminal activities, however it could use a refresh. It's kind of stuck in the 90's, but I loved it all the same. I didn't like all the MS Win homage within a Linux or Unix terminal game. It's a simple version of the rich Linux OS (or Unix) and it's tools as well as the network concept. Which is fine, however the breaking into systems kind of gets old after the third or forth try. You learn that you have to acquire the tool for the job (port) and that's it. You acquire tools as you go, and you "steal" tools as you progress, but it's really simple. It's great all the same, just needs a few adjustments and improvements.

I though you could sell all that data or exchange it for tools, so I kept some of it from the big jobs, I ended up with a tone of stuff in / and /home, never being able to do anything with it.

What the game misunderstands, but makes easy on the player is:
- Unix and Linux binary files don't end in exe and don't use PE format, they use ELF.
- braking firewalls and proxy (well VPN servers) is not that easy and doesn't require any memory on the client/hacker side
- tracing a hacker is done differently, one could kick a user from his machine but not trace him in that way or that fast
- buffer overflow is simplistic and unimaginative 
- the memory concept could've been done differently with memory updates, etc. I expected more, it's just there to make your work slower so the tracer could kick in.
- Unix commands are not uppercase, and are case sensitive (I know, I know, I'm pushing it)
- firewalls and proxys are just there to make you slower, no concept of network or network security

Other Cons:
- no vi (yeah, I kept tying it all the same, and wondered why it didn't work), you have to use cat, replace
- you cannot create folders, no mkdir, which is weird
- no vi so, text editing, you have to kind of use replace, which works for the mostpart
- no touch, so you cannot make new files
- no shell scripts (shell is just a different concept all together)
- /home/ doesn't have a user, AT ALL
- root is admin
- no concept of mount or a filesystem
- no killall command
- there are no routers (because the game acts like we are in the 90's, but there are software firewalls and proxys)
- no VPN concept within the proxy
- no ssh shelling to the other machines and attacking from that machine (override doesn't count, you still have your own IP)
- ssh is just there because
- there are no worms, viruses or rootkits
- forkbomb is just a hard reboot
- the trigger/trap is a waste, you just need it once and never again, you don't even have to have the shells open in the other parts of the game and in the DLC
- the music, although OK for the mostpart, it's a little to digital for me and I kind of require more tones, metal or rock would 
suffice
- there are a few good tracks which have melody inside
- the game hinders CPU extensively (I'm playing it on Linux and this shouldn't happen), it could use with some optimization. I didn't notice this until I minimized the game, or went to shell to do something and saw the CPU cores all at 100% all the while the game was suspended, which is strange. I don't know how it was written, but these things only happen with Javascript.
- the IRC logs are old and outdated, from bash.org
- why do we even have IRC without being able to log and hack it?
- hexclock just randomly changes color as the time ticks, instead of being able you use -s or -n, which don't do anything, to change the hex color yourself.
- not all the save files sync via cloud for me, so I could not enjoy it on different machines, and had to copy the save files manually
- you cannot change the layout of the theme, switch the windows around and change color, leaving you with unwanted colors and layout for most of the time
- DLC themes are better than the original game
- Honeypot theme (you know which server I'm talking about) is just the GOLD theme - which you can acquire before attacking that server
- you don't have to actually delete the logs, it's just so you can complete the job
- no world interaction whatsoever, feels like the machines you break in have no owner and have been sitting there for ages (only one or two cases are dangerous, if we include the DLC, you will actually have to remain unnoticed, rest of the time you can do whatever you like) 
- even though the story starts good, the plot kind of goes off into another corner
- the hacknet program does nothing, and is just there for the plots sake, or in reference to the actual game binary
- there is no concept of money, you just hack for the sake of it
- DLC starting requires research, you have to start it via in-game plot points (it's triggered after you end the game, but it's stated no where how to turn it on)

Pros
- everything else is pro, which is alot
- you can scan for other machines within the network
- the terminal only theme and the network nods make it a great visual pleasure (for us Linux users at least)
- there are secrets within the game
- there are some pieces of the game that will make you feel like you're in a movie
- there are some well though out scenarios - including the DLC
- iOS, or eOS is present, so mobile hacking is possible although very simple and dull
- mobile hacking, pacemaker hacking, other medical devices (although they use the same tool)
- server secrets
- secret servers :D
- great ending (and DLC continuation)
- Neo? - or did I make a mistake (you know what I mean)
- there are some text files or manual documentation for the tools
- you can hack your ISP provider as well
- you can hack almost anything, with a few machines left unbreakable, I won't spoil it
- DLC is really good, so get that too

Advice:
Rename all your commands to the Unix style (all Linux people know what I'm saying) and be lightning fast and untraceable. That's what I did along with placing everything in / and not /home/ which doesn't have a user and is just weird.

Now make yourself some coffee and hack.

Enjoy.

review_text_raw:
Good: 
[list]
    [*]the command line UI is accurate, and makes you feel a lot like a real hacker.
    [*]nice music
    [*]lots of little easter eggs
    [*]technically very accurate (uses correct port numbers, IP addresses, and more)
[/list]

Bad: 
[list]
   [*]core gameplay is extremely repetitive and time consuming (which is an awful combination)
[/list]

The core gameplay of Hacknet revolves around you, a hacker, who can run several different programs to hack into a server and complete some task for a client. For example, hacking into the fried chicken chain CFC server and stealing the list of 11 secret herbs and spices.

It's an interesting concept to start with, however the game falls extremely short in that the gameplay never evolves into anything that is challenging or involves meaningful decision making. 

Hacking each server in the entire game is exactly the same. That is no exaggeration. You literally do the exact same 3-7 things for each server you encounter in order to hack into it. And the worst part about this process is that the "hacking" requires no user interaction. You simply wait 1-2 minutes for the hacking programs to finish, and then you complete whatever task you were assigned to do on the server.

At no point do you need to make any in game decisions when hacking. At no point do you have any decision to make that can affect the gameplay. And that's really where it all falls apart for me. What am I really doing in this game? Because the game really lacks in the feeling of accomplishment.

I can completely understand how this gameplay can appeal to people who want to feel like a hacker, because the game definitely hits the mark in that regard. But once you get past that, you realise there is very little "gameplay" to be had. It just feels like a demo.

review_text_raw:
[b]A HACKER GROUP SEARCHING THE TRUTH[/b]
[i]Hacknet[/i] was available for free in Humble Bundle for a short period, long time ago. It's one of those game that normally I wouldn't buy. The game is centered on group of hackers that receives some contracts from people that wants to obtain something: it could be retrieving a file or cancel something from another user computer. For the entire game, you will see the Hacknet OS, a system that allows to execute some tools and let you inside other networks and devices.

[h1]VERY REPETITIVE GAMEPLAY[/h1]
At the beginning [i]Hacknet[/i] seems promising. The game make you feel like you are a real hacker, trying to break in other people computers, but after a while everything repeat itself. You always do the same things: hack devices ports, with specific executables that you just need to download from the hacker group server, once you are in, you need to check the files, and once you completed the task, simply reply to the client request mail, with details needed. Some of these contract are challenging and it will take a lot of time, trying to understand which is the solution of the enigma. Usually there is not only one way to go, but you can complete the mission in different ways. The real problem is that missions are all the same and nothing really change for the whole game.

[h1]CANCEL THE LOGS[/h1]
One of the things that the game never stop to stress you out is deleting the logs in a computer after you finished to snoop around. At the beginning I did it, because I was scared that I could be traced, losing the mission. After a while, because you have so many steps to do in order to complete the contract, I forgot to clean them several times, and nothing happened. They cannot trace me so I simply stopped to worry about it: I canceled only when I remembered.

[h1]CONCLUSION[/h1]
[i]Hacknet[/i] could have potential. It looks different and interesting, but, as I've mentioned before, you need to do always the same bunch of actions, and this made me lose the interest in the game. I have still to complete the main story, but I think I played enough to express an opinion on this title. I really wanted to buy also DLCs, but after this experience, I think I stop here my experience with this game.

The game is fun.  It has both a GUI and commandline for whichever you are most comfortable with.  At a couple parts, the more intrepid players will find things beyond their means or things they are supposed to discover a little later after explanation that they do not really know what to do with, but that's fine.  I like games that allow you to do that.  There are a lot of funny/entertaining logs to read and it's apparent that there is a lot of thought that went into the story behind it.

Gameplay-wise, though, it wasn't as much as it could be.  A couple hours into it and I realize I'm basically just playing Linux with some commands missing.  That isn't to say I'm not entertained so far, definitely worth it to buy, but if you're familiar with Linux and know your way around the terminal, it won't be anything new and the lack of commands can be a little jarring once you get in your groove.

Another thing, it's definitely a GPU hog.  My GPU was going nuts, especially if I alt-tabbed.  Was getting up to 90c with fans going max.

Overall, though, good game, is fun.  Plan on finishing it when I get some more time to play.

review_text_raw:
*Got the game for $2.99 during a sale*

Hacknet is an interesting game. Let's just get that out of the way. Its got a very good storyline and, while I have some experience in [strike]hacking[/strike] computer security, I didn't find (most) of the puzzles too difficult for the average person to solve. It sets a very good pace, picking up the difficulty very well. I'm writing this review just after completing the game, which took me just over 6 hours.

You start off with a message from Bit, telling you how to use the Hacknet software, etc. etc. Basically a tutorial on how to use it, the command line, that sort of thing. (If you're a linux user, this game will be much easier, the commands are basically the same for navigating the terminal and the like) After this, you're sent off to a hacker group, Entropy. You do a few hacks, and things start to pick up. You rise to the top (naturally) and start going off, investigating. I'd say more but I don't want to risk spoilers. The ending was very intriguing, and worth the effort.

The challenges are similar, but I never got bored of them. Find server at X IP, break down any proxies, firewalls, and open ports to use the almighty PortHack and get the admin password. Then, do whatever you need to, be it uploading or downloading a file, deleting stuff, or (later) even messing with databases and some... other devices. ([spoiler]a pacemaker[/spoiler]) They become more difficult as you progress, adding tracers that initiate an IP change failsafe if you take too long, more ports to open, and more complex firewalls and proxies. You'll need to grab passwords from emails and circumvent servers with powerful tracers, and even more interesting events. The only randomly difficult challenge that jumped me was an attack on my PC, which I was able to avoid using a [spoiler]trap shell[/spoiler]. If it gets you, there is a guide to help you out.

The interface is very intuitive and I never had any unreasonable issues with it, aside from becoming stuck when entering a password I didn't want to enter. (Which is my fault, I clicked login. What did I expect?) Later, you get the option to switch your layout, but none of them are really terrible. You have the terminal window (for commands), the display window (for showing the filesystem, passwords, databases, emails, etc.), the RAM window (watch this one, especially later when you get more RAM-hungry programs), and your NetMap (showing all the IPs you've connected to/can connect to).

The playtime was a good length. I would have liked it to be a bit longer but 6 hours is longer than AAA campaigns. God I hate AAA companies. Be innovative. Or I'll use Hacknet to take down your servers. /rant. Anyway, I'm not complaining about the length. As I said earlier, it never got repetitive, it was always interesting. There was always a sense of "oh gotta do this quickly or they're gonna catch me with that trace" that pushes you forward. Because of that speed though, don't play this game if you're not a quick typist. I have a speed of about 70 WPM (Faster now), which is well above average. I'd recommend being able to go above 40 WPM to play this effectively. 

------------------------------------------------------

Of course, what's a review without a pro/con list.

Pros:
+Good, interesting gameplay
+Active modding community (for extra levels and whatnot)
+Great value for the price (Yes, I know I got it for $2.99. But it's worth the full $9.99)
+Nice visuals (watch out, 1 looks like lowercase L. Tripped me up once)
+Easter Egg bash.org quotes
+Amazing soundtrack. Reflects the mood and urgency of the situations. 10/10 on that.

Neutrals:
+-Console window pops up behind game (Alt Tabbing is a little wierd)
+-Can't skip ending credits

Cons:
-You need to be a quick and accurate typist
-Requires some prior knowledge of terminal commands in order to be efficient (from the start)

------------------------------------------------------

TL; DR

Very interesting, non-repetitive gameplay and a good storyline. Visuals are of high quality and the soundtrack is amazing. However, to be good at this game you should be good at typing ( >40 WPM) and know how to navigate the Linux terminal, or at least pick up on it quickly. (I mean, it's just ls, cd, cat, and mv really) Also, bash.org quotes.

-----------------------------------------------------------------------
UPDATE
-----------------------------------------------------------------------

I've just finished the Hacknet: Labyrinths DLC. I'm adding a short little note here about that.

Definetely worth it. Took an extra 3 and a half hours or so to complete, so pretty decent playtime. Much more interesing puzzles than the base game. You are tasked with completing the "Kaguya Trials" from the CSEC list, and join with a group of 3 other hackers. You'll take missions from a list and complete them with the help of the others. While you usually never actually interact with them other than seeing them in the IRC, it does feel like they're helping you. (I won't spoil how, but it becomes apparent in the endgame.) The challenges were a bit more difficult, but nothing that wasn't impossible. A mission towards the end just becomes a cat-and-mouse chase for a password, but while it didn't seem to guide you it wasn't that difficult to follow the clues. Overall, I'd highly rate the DLC. If you have the extra cash when buying Hacknet, I would recommend purchasing it. Do complete it after the main game though, or your NetMap will become a mess...

------------------------------------------------------

TL; DR

Very well done game and a great expansion to the original. I would definitely recommend purchasing this alongside the base game. Just... Play it after you beat the base game.

review_text_raw:
Got the game for free and it has been sitting in my backlog for a while. Some while ago I finally decided to clear this game with high expectations seeing it receive a lot of positive reviews. Unfortunately I was faced with only disappointment.

At first the gameplay is intriguing and engaging. The terminal style UI certainly looks cool. There are quests that procedurally guide you through the mechanics of the game, and the discovery process keeps the gameplay fresh, but not for long until you join the hacker organization.

From that point what you do is just repeating the same hacking routine again and again, and it gets repetitive very quickly. At this point the only thing left that can do some good for this game is the story. My last hope for the game was that after hours of labour I would uncover traces of a big conspiracy that leads me to something like stopping a skynet, or fighting myself in a moral conflict, you get the meaning.

But no! The main plot is linear and doesn't have much depth to it. It was so uninspiring that I didn't even know I came to the end of the story, just after I did the usual hacking stuff I was greeted with a voice recording and I was like "is that it?".

Also the 'hacking experience' is far from realistic. But I guess it serves the point of letting people feel like they're a hacker.

I really want to like this game, but I couldn't. The music is good though, I think it's the only plus side.

TL;DR: Cool hacking-look UI, repetitive hacking routine, weak story

review_text_raw:
"Real Hacking
Based on actual UNIX commands, Hacknet focuses on real hacking, not the Hollywood-style version of it. This creates a truly immersive experience and puts players right in the thick of trying to break through the firewalls."

Blatant lies. Hacknet is straight up Hollywood hacking. The terminal is a simplistic cross-breed between bash and cmd.exe. It puts you in the role of a script kiddy, who "hacks" systems by observing which ports are open on the target machine and running the corresponding hacking program by typing its name and a port number (e.g. "FTPHack 21"). Once you're in, your job is to either snoop through some files for a password, to download files, or to delete them using basic terminal skills. You're supposed to cover your tracks by deleting logs, but it rarely matters. The same thing, over and over, no brains required. There's no sense you're accomplishing anything of value, nor of any consequence to yourself or others.

It's an insult to anyone with more than a surface-level understanding of network security, as challenging to a puzzle gamer as 50 consecutive games of Tic-tac-toe, and isn't even that interesting in terms of Hollywood hacking simulations. It's on par with a budding game developer's first project, not something worth spending $10 to $24 on. If you want an intellectual challenge (Hollywood setting, but real problem-solving), check out Zachtronics (Exapunks, Shenzhen I/O, TIS-100).

That said, Hacknet does have a few high points. The music is pretty great. The Labyrinths DLC is slightly less mediocre, but isn't worth the regular $7 price point on top of the base game's $10. If everything was like the DLC's final mission — which unexpectedly drops you into a timed, high-stakes situation with dire consequences — this might actually be a decent game. As is, though, it's just a bland waste of money.

review_text_raw:
[h1][i][b][u]Hacknet - 8/10[/u][/b][/i][/h1]

[u]Story[/u]
Hacknet is a puzzle game that focuses mainly on, well, hacking! At the very start of the game, you get a message from a person called "Bit", requesting a bit of hacking. [spoiler]He then, in a way, requests you to investigate his death.[/spoiler] There are also a bunch of "side" missions if you can call them that, to get good with a few other groups. I'm not saying anything else, go play it and experience it for yourself. The story is amazing and has a weird type of ending. Satisfying, though.
[spoiler]By the way, if you already know computer commands or you know how to hack, then you can skip the tutorial by writing "ps" once you get hold of the console and then "kill [i][Number shown beside "Tutorial"]"[/i][/spoiler]
[spoiler]You don't have to clear logs unless it tells you to do so in the mission briefing.[/spoiler]

[u]Storyline Length[/u]
This all depends on how good you are at puzzles, what knowledge you have of computer commands, and how fast you type. If you're great at all three of things, like me, then it should take you about an hour or two. There are quite a few tricky parts, so it might take you longer. If you're an achievement hunter, this will require at least two playthroughs to unlock all the achievements.

[u]AI[/u]
I'm not too sure if this counts as AI, but if you start to hack a really secure place, there's a chance you'll start to get traced. You have ninety seconds to finish up (and for some reason those 'ninety seconds' always go at a different speed) or else you have another minute or so to change your IP. Also, you can reply to emails and kill a guy or two but they don't really count as AI. Not in this game, anyway.

[u]Experience[/u]
This game will make you feel like a true hacker. Opening the ports of a secure server has never been easier with the programmes and knowledge you have! Firewalls? Not a problem! Proxy? Easy. 5 ports to open? Kindergarten stuff. This game, from start to finish, is a wild ride.  It'll make you laugh, make you make a hard decision even though you kinda have to do it one way, make you feel like everyone else is a peasant and you're the superior. You know, just like winning a round of CS:GO competitive against nine year olds. You can't have too many stuff open at once, which makes this game really challenging sometimes. Especially when you have to change your IP and you're extremely stressed. I'm not sure if you can move them around, I haven't tried, but the area where you decide where to connect to gets [i]extremely[/i] cluttered after a while. Would be great if you can delete some circles you're absolutely sure you won't connect to again.
Anyway, this thing actually runs on cmd which makes you feel even more of a hacker.
[spoiler]If you write "OpenCDTray" then it will open your actual computer's CD tray if you have one. Pretty damn cool![/spoiler]

[u]Graphics[/u]
Well, it's a computer desktop. Not much else to say. Deep into the game, you can get a theme changer, which changes your desktop in-game. That's about it, really.

[u]Sound[/u]
The soundtrack is not bad at all. It fits the game and can actually be quite relaxing! Although, you'll probably hear your keyboard half the time. Good stuff!

[u]Overall[/u]
I'd recommend this game to pretty much anyone. Especially those who love puzzle games, like me. This has a great story, challenging puzzles at times, and a great end. The achievements aren't too hard, but they're not too easy. Pick this up if you can, definitely worth €10.

[u]Specs[/u]
Well, it's a game that's literally cmd with a pretty desktop. I'm pretty sure the oldest computer on Earth could run this.

[spoiler]By the way, if you already know computer commands or you know how to hack, then you can skip the tutorial by writing "ps" once you get hold of the console and then "kill [i][Number shown beside "Tutorial"]"[/i][/spoiler] [spoiler]You don't have to clear logs unless it tells you to do so in the mission briefing.[/spoiler] [u]Storyline Length[/u] This all depends on how good you are at puzzles, what knowledge you have of computer commands, and how fast you type. If you're great at all three of things, like me, then it should take you about an hour or two. There are quite a few tricky parts, so it might take you longer. If you're an achievement hunter, this will require at least two playthroughs to unlock all the achievements. [u]AI[/u] I'm not too sure if this counts as AI, but if you start to hack a really secure place, there's a chance you'll start to get traced. You have ninety seconds to finish up (and for some reason those 'ninety seconds' always go at a different speed) or else you have another minute or so to change your IP. Also, you can reply to emails and kill a guy or two but they don't really count as AI. Not in this game, anyway. [u]Experience[/u] This game will make you feel like a true hacker. Opening the ports of a secure server has never been easier with the programmes and knowledge you have! Firewalls? Not a problem! Proxy? Easy. 5 ports to open? Kindergarten stuff. This game, from start to finish, is a wild ride. It'll make you laugh, make you make a hard decision even though you kinda have to do it one way, make you feel like everyone else is a peasant and you're the superior. You know, just like winning a round of CS:GO competitive against nine year olds. You can't have too many stuff open at once, which makes this game really challenging sometimes. Especially when you have to change your IP and you're extremely stressed. I'm not sure if you can move them around, I haven't tried, but the area where you decide where to connect to gets [i]extremely[/i] cluttered after a while. Would be great if you can delete some circles you're absolutely sure you won't connect to again. Anyway, this thing actually runs on cmd which makes you feel even more of a hacker. [spoiler]If you write "OpenCDTray" then it will open your actual computer's CD tray if you have one. Pretty damn cool![/spoiler] [u]Graphics[/u] Well, it's a computer desktop. Not much else to say. Deep into the game, you can get a theme changer, which changes your desktop in-game. That's about it, really. [u]Sound[/u] The soundtrack is not bad at all. It fits the game and can actually be quite relaxing! Although, you'll probably hear your keyboard half the time. Good stuff! [u]Overall[/u] I'd recommend this game to pretty much anyone. Especially those who love puzzle games, like me. This has a great story, challenging puzzles at times, and a great end. The achievements aren't too hard, but they're not too easy. Pick this up if you can, definitely worth €10. [u]Specs[/u] Well, it's a game that's literally cmd with a pretty desktop. I'm pretty sure the oldest computer on Earth could run this. review_text_raw:
Overview:
  Hacknet is at its heart a digital exploration game. Using a powerful suite of programs that you gain throughout the game, the player must gain access to systems and perform contracts. The game has a very similar feeling to the older game Uplink and hacking is done through speed, knowledge of your tools, and system resource management (RAM).

Plot:
  The plot is pretty threadbare, but does a good job of pulling the overarching story together. The ending makes sense, but is a little lacklustre for the scope of what you supposedly accomplish. However, this is in character for hacking since public attention is bad for those at the fringe of legality. Overall, I enjoyed the plot, but the beginning intro and ending are really the only interesting points. It's difficult to do characterization when all you have is text, but I felt that more effort could have been put into letting the player get to know more of the other people in the story (naix, maybe some backstory on bit, etc.)
 
Gameplay:
  The gameplay is separated into two parts: hacking and forensics. The actual hacking is rather easy since most trace timers last far more than long enough and some systems actually keep your admin after you disconnect. The main challenge in this format is simply knowing which order to run the port hacking programs in so that you can maximize efficiency and minimize time spent not logged in. These do get quite intense at times and a few conflict sequences definitely run the point home that you're not invulnerable. Progress through the game is blocked in a sort of metroid-vania way, in the sense that you need this power to unlock that type of port to enter. I enjoyed this, but wished that there were more early systems that you needed to backtrack to.

  That backtracking is part of the second part of the gameplay, the forensics. By this I mean that you spend your time going through file systems trying to spot the file with the password, scanning computers to reach connected nodes, and searching for new IPs to check out. In fact, there is an entirely alternative gameplay path that is only reached with diligent use of your tools. I loved the exploring, but it did feel quite limited, or at the very least truncated to be more accessable for players who might not be used to the gameplay style.
  Part of the joy of the exploration comes from the humor that you find in random files. From a script for "Titanic 2" that involves the icebergs running onto land and attacking people to Bash.org IRC logs, there is a decent amount of silliness and joy to discover. However, since the files in the systems you hack are procedurally generated, more content would have been nice. There's only so many times that you can see the same Bash log before you stop wanting 
to check them out because you feel you've seen everything.

Pros:
*really fun
*sense of satisfaction from difficult hacks
*humor: From a mission where you need to write "d*cks" on the main webpage of "Nortron Security" to an homage to *chans (the secret /el/ image board), the game is very funny and self aware.
*exploration
*failure penalty fair
*short: Hacknet doesn't wear out its welcome, which it probably would have for some players by the end game.

Cons:
*repetitive
*short
*not enough content
*exploration feels like it was stunted for ease of access

Hopes:
*mods:
	I feel that mods could make this from a good game to a great game. I'd love to try my hand at adding new features to the game.
*hardware changes
	Uplink let the player purchase hardware upgrades to increase ram or processing power as well as giving access to more complicated systems. Hacknet's only customization for your computer is changing the display theme.
*more story
	Getting to know the other hackers more personally would be very enjoyable.
*higher difficulty
	clearing the logs on a system means that they won't track you down - but this presents a problem. You always leave a disconnect log, but the game doesn't notice that a disconnect log without a matching connect log implies
	that the IP that disconnected was responsible for the attack. Having to selectively clear logs and/or bounce IP like Uplink might be a good idea. In addition, I would have enjoyed more difficult forensics and encrypted files
	that you can't find the password for. I was a little miffed a few times when I spent some time looking through the files to find the next IP when all I had to do was type "scan". More threats to the player as well as uncertainty
	in how well you performed the attack would be welcome.
*more challenges
	Maybe adding in new network architecture requiring the player to do a different minigame than typing the first two letters of a program and tab completing.
*multiplayer
	multiplayer is hinted at being in development in the files on the endgame server.

Bottom Line:
I love this game and want to spend so much more time on it, but sadly it seems that there's no more content. This type of game is sadly lacking in today's market and is quite unique. It pulls off what it does well and with much better guidance than Uplink. You should try it if you're interested in learning basic cmd/*nix commands and command line navigation/use while having fun, if you like tech and silly games, or if you're a fan of Uplink.

review_text_raw:
Overall, it's a repetitive, but very visually and aurally satisfying, clicker/visual novel game. The best features are meant for multiplayer. You're warned to wipe logs early in the game, but logs are useless since there isnt anyone to read them (I stopped clearing them about halfway). Many of the features (like "forkbomb" and the trap functionality of the shells) are completely useless without multiplayer. There are no enemy hackers (save one, who is a major story character and only attempts to hack you once). The world is not alive. It is essentially a visual novel treasure hunt, where you go from one node to the next, doing the same things over and over with the incentive to just finish the game. The story and storytelling arent even good enough to justify it being this way. Maybe when it has multiplayer, itll be worth playing. Overall, the feeling of urgency isn't there like it would be if you were playing a game like slavehack.

When it gets multiplayer, if the multiplayer works correctly, it could well be one of the funnest and most exciting hacking games ever. Until then, unless you think the idea of writing commands instead of doing the same exact thing with a mouse is a good experience, I would probably just get uplink.

Also, if you're reading this review devs, Duckman should be expanded on. He's easily the best character in the game. Thanks Duckfam, you unsung hero.

review_text_raw:
You are a curious hacker. You get a message from someone claiming to be a fellow hacker who has uncovered a dark secret, and chances are since we’re reading this message they are now dead. You’re going to have to get in the driver's seat and pick up the pieces left by this hacker and uncover what is really going on. As you progress through the game you’re going to be given additional tools that you’ll need to unlock the harder to break into systems, and you’ll also be forced with moral decisions, but the life of a hacker is never easy in HackNet.

I will fully admit that when I first started playing this game I was both overwhelmed and underwhelmed. I was excited to see where the story was going to take me, but at the same time the mechanics of the game definitely requires some time to get proficient at it. You see you’re going to be attacking this game through a terminal view. You will have a map of different machines that you can hit, a command prompt, and on some occasion some graphical interface that you’re going to be able to navigate with. This game is going to test your ability to type out commands, the correct ones, many times within a time limit. You will have to navigate through file directories to uncover the information that you’re looking for, and at the same time you’re going to have to erase your footprints in each system’s log file directory.

In order to dig deeper and deeper into the mystery that is at the center of the story you’re going to have to discover hacker groups, you’re going to have to pass their tests, and you’re also going to have to complete tasks for those groups in order to build up trust. With that trust you’ll be given other programs that you can use to crack tougher systems, and also with that trust you’re going to have to face some moral decisions that may end up haunting you as a result. Sometimes the game feels a little too real, especially when the “system” reboots and there’s that second or two of “holy crap did I break my actual computer?” floating through your mind.

If you are looking for blood and guts, this is not the game for you. If you are looking for a straight forward story, this is not the game for you. In complete honesty there are parts of this game that left me scratching my head simply because I didn’t know what to do next and had to stumble around trying random things until it stuck. It is possible to complete the game without taking on every single hacker request, but I personally think that there’s a chance you’ll benefit from the extra practice. Speaking of practice, this is definitely not a game you can pick up from time to time. This is a game you’re going to want to go at as quickly as you can. I can’t stress enough about how much time is a factor in this game, and the mountain of extra stuff you have to do in order to “right the ship” if the timer were to run out.

I’m happy to say that I was able to play through this entire game, it took me just under 6 hours, but I was able to do it. The strange thing is that outside of my relief and feeling of accomplishment, I can honestly say I don’t know if I can recommend this game or tell you to stay away from it. It was an experience, something that tested me, and I was able to win in the end, I just don’t know what to make of it at the end of the day. As a reviewer this is one of the most frustrating mindsets to find one’s self in, and it is exactly that mindset that I find myself in.

review_text_raw:
What a great game. I acquired this in a Humble Bundle recently with a few other titles. Without looking, I assumed it was just a game that was shoveled in to fluff out the bundle, and that I wouldn't enjoy it. I ended up loving it, and I'm definitely going to buy the DLC (and likely any more content that may come out for Hacknet in the future).

Hacknet, for lack of better words, is a Unix-based hacking simulator in which you use the combination of a point-and-click interface and a command prompt to explore the mysterious death of a hacker named "Bit." Bit has arranged to send automated messages to you posthumously, giving you leads that are just enough for you to find your way.

Being not much of a programmer, and unfamiliar with Linux and Unix-based command systems (idk man I just look stuff up and punch shit into the Windows 10 command prompt and sometimes it says words back to me), I felt learning to play Hacknet might be too daunting of a task. However, the feeling subsided in less than half an hour, when I was able to navigate through any device's file systems with ease, hopping from device to device, opening ports, cracking passwords, etc. Not long after that was I very immersed in the story (something I have a hard time being in MANY games).

While some aspects of the game can be done through clicking between devices, folders, and apps, other things are seemingly only possible by using the command-line, keeping the game immersive and making you feel, in a sense, accomplished. YOU cracked open all of Macrosoft's ports and got to snoop around in their sensitive files. YOU found a security loophole by exploiting a computer's connected smartphone. YOU made a clean getaway just in time before having your IP traced, clearing the system logs and running for the hills with some juicy new program you can use to hack *even more* devices. And you did it all with your analytical skills and an intuitive command system. In fact, there's even a point in the game where your OS/interface is essentially deleted from your system by another angry hacker, leaving you with a big black command terminal, having to plot through your own computer to restore the deleted files and get yourself back in the game. Just like in real life, each device you access seems like a sum of its parts, even your own.

The IP tracing mechanic is excellent, and pretty much exactly what you'd imagine seeing on some Hollywood hacker's monitor. It keeps the pressure on, even if it is slow at times. RAM management, learning what ports to use when, and being able to type quickly and remember which programs do what are important, and make hacking into each and every system rewarding in its own way, even if it doesn't have quite what you were looking for.

The visual effects are excellent, if a bit cheesy at times. The interface is simple enough that these "glitchy" or "tech-y" effects aren't too jarring unless they need to be, which keeps the game immersive but also fun to watch. I'd advise that anyone with epilepsy be careful with this game at some times - lots of effects are fast or flashy in nature.

The story doesn't seem to thrust itself into your face at all. Save for the occasional automated (but justified) email from Bit, you discover all of the story on your own, and every lead and new piece of information feels genuine and is worth discovering.

Overall, I had a lot of fun with this game. Two complaints (which end up not really being complaints after I explain them):

- The IP map, showing all known devices and their IPs, can get a bit cluttered, and it's easy to forget where one particular computer is on the big web of spinning circles and lines connecting them. The position of an IP address on the map is not always intuitive. However, this could arguably help with immersion, making you feel like you're navigating through a web of IP addresses. It's the internet in its raw form - not catered to your viewing pleasure.

- I'm left wanting more. Not that I didn't get my money's worth, but I want more. But that's something every game should strive for - leaving you wanting more, and not outstaying its welcome.

Challenging, but *very* rewarding command system that makes you feel clever. Decent story that keeps you invested throughout the game. Findable humorous IRC logs, detailing early Internet culture, which I think are ripped straight from Bash.org, meaning they are real logs written by real people. Stereotypical electronic "hacker" soundtrack which helps the atmosphere of the game.

If any of this interests you, definitely get Hacknet, especially if it's in a bundle or on sale.

Being not much of a programmer, and unfamiliar with Linux and Unix-based command systems (idk man I just look stuff up and punch shit into the Windows 10 command prompt and sometimes it says words back to me), I felt learning to play Hacknet might be too daunting of a task. However, the feeling subsided in less than half an hour, when I was able to navigate through any device's file systems with ease, hopping from device to device, opening ports, cracking passwords, etc. Not long after that was I very immersed in the story (something I have a hard time being in MANY games). While some aspects of the game can be done through clicking between devices, folders, and apps, other things are seemingly only possible by using the command-line, keeping the game immersive and making you feel, in a sense, accomplished. YOU cracked open all of Macrosoft's ports and got to snoop around in their sensitive files. YOU found a security loophole by exploiting a computer's connected smartphone. YOU made a clean getaway just in time before having your IP traced, clearing the system logs and running for the hills with some juicy new program you can use to hack *even more* devices. And you did it all with your analytical skills and an intuitive command system. In fact, there's even a point in the game where your OS/interface is essentially deleted from your system by another angry hacker, leaving you with a big black command terminal, having to plot through your own computer to restore the deleted files and get yourself back in the game. Just like in real life, each device you access seems like a sum of its parts, even your own. The IP tracing mechanic is excellent, and pretty much exactly what you'd imagine seeing on some Hollywood hacker's monitor. It keeps the pressure on, even if it is slow at times. RAM management, learning what ports to use when, and being able to type quickly and remember which programs do what are important, and make hacking into each and every system rewarding in its own way, even if it doesn't have quite what you were looking for. The visual effects are excellent, if a bit cheesy at times. The interface is simple enough that these "glitchy" or "tech-y" effects aren't too jarring unless they need to be, which keeps the game immersive but also fun to watch. I'd advise that anyone with epilepsy be careful with this game at some times - lots of effects are fast or flashy in nature. The story doesn't seem to thrust itself into your face at all. Save for the occasional automated (but justified) email from Bit, you discover all of the story on your own, and every lead and new piece of information feels genuine and is worth discovering. Overall, I had a lot of fun with this game. Two complaints (which end up not really being complaints after I explain them): - The IP map, showing all known devices and their IPs, can get a bit cluttered, and it's easy to forget where one particular computer is on the big web of spinning circles and lines connecting them. The position of an IP address on the map is not always intuitive. However, this could arguably help with immersion, making you feel like you're navigating through a web of IP addresses. It's the internet in its raw form - not catered to your viewing pleasure. - I'm left wanting more. Not that I didn't get my money's worth, but I want more. But that's something every game should strive for - leaving you wanting more, and not outstaying its welcome. Challenging, but *very* rewarding command system that makes you feel clever. Decent story that keeps you invested throughout the game. Findable humorous IRC logs, detailing early Internet culture, which I think are ripped straight from Bash.org, meaning they are real logs written by real people. Stereotypical electronic "hacker" soundtrack which helps the atmosphere of the game. If any of this interests you, definitely get Hacknet, especially if it's in a bundle or on sale.

review_text_raw:
How would hacking be without knowledge, skills or creativity? 

The same "hacks" get applied repetitively to open ports and then read/download/delete files over and over again. I've seen more challenging escape rooms.

Don't get me wrong - It's amazing for an indie game developed by one person. But on the other hand there are CTFs with a nice story out there that keep me busy without making me feel like in a hamster wheel. If you are into cyber security, don't waste your time with this. 

But if you have zero knowledge and want to feel like a hacker, this game teaches a few basics about handling a Linux-like OS (with wine for .exe files) and simulates how to move through a network.

It would be great to focus on only a few stories and individualize the targets instead of seeing generic ancient bash content on every PC. Also I missed a proper C2 setup with own proxies that I can create, privilege escalation and lateral movement instead of being admin immediately, alternating attack vectors and the option to create scripts or at least files ("touch") and directories ("mkdir"). This would have been a nice starting point to start playing around, break things out of curiosity and discover the possibilities instead of moving inside the box all the time.
